findings.message: `defmt` was removed from the default features, and the PR description doesn't mention it. Downstream crates that use the defaults and depend on `Error<E>: defmt::Format` (or log it with defmt) will stop compiling. This is a breaking API change unrelated to PartitionGuard. Revert it, or call it out and handle it as a semver-breaking change.

`lock()`/`try_lock()` lock the mutex for the whole storage device, not just this partition. While a PartitionGuard is alive, every other partition (and the same `Partition` through its own trait methods, which call `self.storage.lock().await`) waits forever if used in the same task. That is an easy self-deadlock to hit, e.g. `let g = p.lock().await; p.read(..).await`. None of this is documented: the doc comments suggest the guard is per-partition. State clearly that the guard locks the whole device and that the partition (and its siblings) must not be used while it is held.

The motivation is to let panic handlers reach storage. But every PartitionGuard operation is `async`, so a synchronous panic handler still needs an executor or `block_on` to use it. Also, if the panicking task held the lock in the middle of a flash operation, `try_lock` fails and the data can't be written anyway. The use case is only partly solved and this isn't documented. Consider documenting the limits, or offering a way to recover or force access.

`start_block` and `check_access` are copied word for word from the `Partition` impl, `within_bounds` is copied in lib.rs (lines 138-148), and the BlockDevice/NorFlash bodies are repeated too. Later fixes to the bounds logic can easily land in one copy and not the other. Move the shared logic into a helper that works on `(offset, size)`, and have both `Partition` and `PartitionGuard` call it.

Behaviour change: `erase(from, to)` with `from > to` used to pass `saturating_sub` = 0 through the bounds check and let the underlying driver report its own error (usually NotAligned or another driver-specific error). It now returns `Error::OutOfBounds`. That may be fine, but it is a silent semantic change to the existing `Partition` API, and the PR doesn't mention or test it.

`#[allow(unused)]` on the public `PartitionGuard` struct (and on its `within_bounds`) hides real dead-code warnings when the `esa`/`bdd` features are off. In that case the guard has no usable methods at all. Gate the guard with `cfg` on those features, or drop the blanket allow.

`Partition<RW>` has `readonly()` to downgrade to RO, but `PartitionGuard<RW>` has no equivalent. So a write-capable guard can't be handed to code that expects a read-only one, and the API is inconsistent. Consider adding `PartitionGuard::readonly`.
